title: Ayyub's call
hook: Ayyub calls, harm has touched me and You are the most merciful, and is healed (21:83–84)
carry: harm touched me; you are merciful

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sulayman and the grazed field, where a father let his son be right. Your line was the young one saw it.

Some prayers are long, with openings and closings and lists. The one in today's verse has two parts, and neither is a request in so many words. A man has lost his health and his family, and commentators add his wealth too. They say the trial went on for years; nobody can tell you exactly how many. When he finally speaks to God about it, he doesn't argue or bargain. He says what happened, and he says who God is. Al-Anbiya keeps it to two verses. Today, the call of Ayyub, the man the Bible calls Job.
screen: `TWO PARTS: WHAT HAPPENED, WHO GOD IS.`

segments.voice: Pickthall gives his words this way: "Lo! adversity afflicteth me, and Thou art Most Merciful of all who show mercy." In Arabic it's short enough to hold in one breath. Massaniya ad-durr: harm has touched me. The verb massa means to touch. He doesn't say harm crushed me. He says it touched me, which some commentators read as courtesy, a man choosing his words carefully even in pain. Then: wa anta arhamu r-rahimin, and You are the most merciful of the merciful. Notice what's missing. There is no heal me. He lays the wound next to the mercy and leaves the rest to God. The next verse says God answered. The harm was removed, and his family given back to him, with the like of them besides, as a mercy and a reminder. Surah Sad adds a little: he is told to strike the ground with his foot, and there is cool water to wash in and drink. And God calls him patient, an excellent servant. That's the surprise. The Qur'an praises Ayyub's patience in the same story where he tells God plainly that he's hurting. So patience here isn't silence. Ya'qub says something close in Surah Yusuf: he takes his grief to God and to no one else. Some scholars draw a line: complaining about God to people is one thing; telling God is part of the prayer. You may have heard longer tales of Ayyub, with details of his illness and his wife. Those are stories people tell, from later collections. The Qur'an itself stays brief.
screen: `HARM HAS TOUCHED ME.` · `YOU ARE THE MOST MERCIFUL.` · `NAMING, NOT PLEADING.` · `PATIENT, AND HONEST ABOUT THE PAIN.`

segments.voice: Find one thing that hurts right now, a worry, a loss, a body that aches, and give it a few plain words, the way Ayyub did, without explaining or arguing. If you pray, you can say his line, harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful, and stop there. If you don't, name the hurt to yourself, kindly, and let it sit beside you.
Ayyub's call. Two parts: harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful. Named, not argued. Today's word.
Your line: harm touched me; you are merciful. Patience can still say where it hurts. That's day four hundred eighty-two.

screen: `DAY 482 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ZAKARIYYA: DON'T LEAVE ME ALONE.`

howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Ayyub's words from 21:83 in times of illness or hardship, often in Arabic, as a short personal supplication alongside the daily prayers.

fork.setup: you've lost your health, your wealth and your family. you finally speak to God about it. what do you say?
options: list everything that went wrong, and ask why.
say harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful.
say nothing at all, to prove you're patient.
fork.reveal: two short parts, and no direct request. God answers anyway, and still calls him patient.

original.note: Arabic: harm has touched me. Ayyub's words in 21:83.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ayyub was patient, so he never complained.
what it means: he told God plainly that harm had touched him, and named God's mercy, and the Qur'an still calls him patient.
what a scholar hears: massa, a light touch, is read by some commentators as adab, courtesy toward God; Ayyub appears in 4:163, 6:84, 21:83–84 and 38:41–44.
recall: gratitude, letting a gift be seen

chat.says: Is it okay to tell God I'm hurting, or does that mean I'm not patient?
options: Ayyub told God plainly that harm touched him, and was still called patient.
Patience means silence; Ayyub never spoke to God about his pain.
Ayyub's patience ran out, so the Qur'an doesn't praise him for it.
chat.meaning: The Qur'an calls Ayyub patient, an excellent servant, in the same story where he says: harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful.

Ayyub.meaning: Job, the prophet tested with long hardship

arhamu r-rahimin.meaning: the most merciful of the merciful

Ya'qub.meaning: Jacob, who took his grief to God

notes: Pickthall wording of 21:83 quoted from memory; please confirm exactly.
The reading of massa as a light touch, chosen out of courtesy, is attributed generally to 'some commentators'; confirm a tafsir source.
'The trial went on for years' and the longer tales of his illness and wife are framed as commentators' reports and stories people tell; confirm framing.
The line about complaining to God being part of prayer (with Ya'qub, 12:86) is a common scholarly point; confirm wording.
The Qur'an mentions his family restored (21:84, 38:43); the loss of wealth comes from tafsir, so the hook now attributes it to commentators. Confirm.

'It doesn't ask for anything' / 'no heal me': many commentators read the call as an implicit request (21:84 says 'We answered him'); the script frames it as asking by naming rather than by a direct plea. A Keeper may want to soften further.
